6876: Men and Women in Church and Home
6877: Does Scripture reserve certain church offices or household responsibilities to men, and if so, on what grounds?
6878:
Every Christian tradition affirms that women and men are equally made in God's image, equally redeemed, and equally gifted by the Spirit. The disagreement is about what follows from that equality. Are there roles in the church (elder, pastor, priest, bishop) or in marriage (headship) that God has assigned to men? If so, is the reason a creation order that Paul invokes, or a sacramental logic in which the priest represents Christ the Bridegroom? If not, are the restrictive passages best explained as local responses to particular problems in Corinth and Ephesus?

Three positions are compared here. Complementarianism (a term coined in the late 1980s) holds that men and women are equal in worth but that Scripture assigns loving male headship in marriage and restricts the elder/pastoral office to qualified men. Egalitarianism holds that Scripture, read as a whole and in context, opens every ministry and household role to both sexes on the basis of gifting and character, and calls husbands and wives to mutual submission. The sacramental view, held officially by the Catholic and Orthodox churches, reserves ordination to the priesthood to men not chiefly because of a hierarchy of authority between the sexes but because the priest acts sacramentally in the person of Christ the Bridegroom; it usually reads marriage in terms of mutual self-gift rather than a chain of command.

The key battlegrounds are a handful of hard Pauline texts (1 Tim 2:11-15, 1 Cor 11:2-16, 1 Cor 14:34-35, Eph 5:21-33), the creation narratives of Gen 1-3, Paul's baptismal declaration in Gal 3:28, and the women leaders named in Scripture: Deborah, Huldah, Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia. Each side has serious scholars, and each side has a history of being caricatured by the other.
6880:
Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity, worth and standing before God, and that God designed them to complement one another with some differing responsibilities. In marriage, the husband is called to loving, servant headship and the wife to intelligent, willing submission; in the church, the office of elder or pastor (the authoritative teaching and governing office) is reserved for qualified men. Women are encouraged in a wide range of ministries, including teaching women and children, prophecy, missions, deaconing in many churches, and public service.

The view is not monolithic. 'Narrow' complementarians apply male headship only to the home and to the eldership, and may allow women to preach under elder oversight, serve as deacons, or lead ministries. 'Broad' complementarians, following John Piper's account of mature masculinity, see a general pattern of male leadership that has implications beyond church and home, though they rarely legislate it. A further spectrum runs from 'hard' to 'soft' complementarians, the latter stressing mutuality in marriage and minimizing the practical difference headship makes. Since 2016 complementarians have also divided over whether headship should be grounded in an eternal submission of the Son to the Father.

6895:
Restrictions on women in church office were near-universal in Christian history, but the modern complementarian position was articulated as a self-conscious evangelical response to 1970s-80s 'biblical feminism'. In December 1987 a group including Piper, Grudem, Wayne House and others met in Danvers, Massachusetts, forming the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood (CBMW) and drafting the Danvers Statement. The term 'complementarian' was chosen to stress equality and difference together, distancing the view from older patriarchal language.

The position was codified in denominational statements such as the Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (Article VI limits the office of pastor to men) and is held by the Presbyterian Church in America, the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and many independent evangelical churches. Debates within the movement concern how far headship extends, whether women may preach, the 2016 controversy over the 'eternal functional subordination' of the Son, and how complementarian churches handle abuse.

6947:
Evangelical egalitarians hold that Scripture, read as a whole and in its historical setting, teaches that men and women are equal not only in worth but in their eligibility for every ministry and household role. Gifting, calling and character, not sex, determine who may preach, pastor, serve as elder or lead. In marriage, husband and wife submit to one another and share authority and responsibility (Eph 5:21; 1 Cor 7:3-4).

Egalitarians generally hold a high view of biblical authority and argue their case exegetically. They read Gen 1-2 as describing partnership, with hierarchy entering as a consequence of the fall (Gen 3:16) that redemption begins to undo. They see Gal 3:28 and the outpouring of the Spirit on sons and daughters (Acts 2:17-18) as the trajectory of the new covenant, and they treat the restrictive texts (1 Cor 14:34-35; 1 Tim 2:11-15) as addressing specific problems in Corinth and Ephesus. They point to women who led, prophesied, taught and served as apostles, deacons and co-workers in Scripture.
